A Compendium of the Narrative of the Marriage of Śrī Padminī.
There was a king named Kāsāra, and his daughter was Padminī;
that king also had a son named Kumudākara.
Upon seeing the form of the prince named Udayadhara depicted in that painting, Padminī herself spontaneously felt a deep attraction toward him, as if he were the sun itself.
But one named Kumudākara, having seen in a painting the form of the daughter of the Moon, became enamored of a woman named Kaumudī.
The evil-minded one named Mattebha brought the young girl under his control for the sake of his own son; having taken the girl himself to his own abode, he held her captive. (4)

The dull-witted one named Jīmūta himself set his heart upon the lotus-pond; he requested it from the affectionate lord of the marshy lands through the mediation of his minister— a certain foolish man, beloved by the snow and surrounded by a circle of frost.
The friend of the intoxicated elephant, who was under his control, prepared to seize the lotus pond;
having observed all this, the lake became greatly distressed.
Having obtained a disciple named Kāśastamba as his surety, he chose the yogin Śāradānanda for the sake of the desired accomplishment of his two sons.
Having reached Udayadhara, he said, "I shall cause your son, named Bhāskara,
to practice the science of archery," and thus he took him as his pupil.
Bhāskara was brought to Kāsārapura by that preceptor; there he witnessed the appearance of darkness produced by a cloud. || 9 ||
The Sun-god slew her as she was striving to conceal her true self;
previously, the gracious Candraśekhara had granted her a lake.
The bud, containing a jewel within, spoke to that king:
"By whomsoever this bud is made to blossom here through touch... (11)
Know him indeed to be the abode of Viṣṇu; he shall become the son-in-law of Aditi.
Taking that bud, he went into the presence of Śāradānanda.
When the sun had grasped that lotus bud with its rays as directed by the Guru’s word,
the self-restrained sage took the jewel from within the opened bud.
Having recognized his greatness, [the Sun] placed the jewel [there], thinking, "I shall give this to him.
There, the Sun, accompanied by Aruṇa, was honored by Kāsāra.
He dwelt in a garden pavilion, cherished by male and female servants;
once, he was together with Padminī and her friend named Bhramarikā.
Afflicted by the pain of separation, she went into the middle of the garden;
while the sun was wandering there, he saw her, though she was concealed by trees.
Then, assuming the form of a companion, the Moon remained with her, knowing her delight,
traveling by means of a mechanical aerial chariot.
Having gone with his wife Himānī to destroy the lotus-pond,
the prince, seeing her terrified, comforted that slender woman.
With its rays, that circle of frost struck down that wicked enemy;
and that mass of snow vowed: "O lotus, I shall do this for you from this day forward."
"Because my beloved has been killed by you, I shall kill you! Thus spoke that yogi Śāradānanda for the sake of accomplishing the desire of Padminī.
"Having taught you the mantra of Śrī, recite it and worship Śrī.
Having said this, she then reached the city of Mattebha on the night of the Kaumudī festival.
Having summoned her, he said this to her for the fulfillment of her desire: "We shall give you a divine image; worship it today, for it is untouched by human hands."
Having spoken thus, by means of mere touch, he transformed the image into the form of a lotus pond and,
having made it a snatcher of those nearby, gave it [to him] through that stratagem.
Longing for the moonlight and seeking union with the bed of night-lotuses,
she worshipped that image with a mantra bestowed by the yogi.
The yogi said to Mattebhaka: "For the sake of the life of the Lord of Kaumudī, one should remain in the vow for three months; let her remain unbroken for that long. (25)
Padminī said to her friend, "Let a golden image of Śrī be placed upon a palanquin and brought to the house of worship. || 26 ||
Then, after consulting with her friend named Madhuvratā, she placed the Sun upon a palanquin in private, together with an image of Lakṣmī.
Having brought him to the place of worship, she caused him to rest somewhere;
then that Padminī, having bathed, worshipped the Mother of the World.
At the conclusion of the worship, that friend Bhāskara departed slowly;
then, approaching her in private, he [spoke of] that which had long been held in his heart.
Embracing her, who was situated between bashfulness and passion, he sported with her at his will;
then Jīmūta arrived with his attendants for the sake of the wedding.
Kāsāra said something based on the words of Śāradānanda:
"For three months starting from the day of her marriage, she shall observe this vow. (31)
"Until she has performed what is for the welfare of her husband, she must not be touched.
Having accepted this, Jīmūta proceeded with the marriage.
Then, on the occasion of the auspicious rite, the yogi said:
"Let my daughter Lakṣmī go to your abode and pay homage to that Goddess. (33)
Likewise, Padminī reached the temple of the Goddess with her female companion;
meanwhile, Kumudākara arrived there together with his male companion. (34)
When those two had arrived, they then exchanged their forms;
he made his companion like a whirlwind to Milinda.
She settled Padminī with her friend in the chamber on the ground;
there she took pleasure with her beloved Bhīta, the son of the Sun.
Then, having taken the hand of such a prince as Jīmūta, that dull-witted man returned with his wife once this marriage was concluded.
Then the yogi himself, in private, began to depart for his own city after summoning Kumudākara, who was accompanied by his friend.
Having kept that means for conquering the enemy in their minds,
the two set out with curiosity, being led by Jīmūta.
Having reached that city, Kumudākara, practicing his vow in seclusion,
worshipped the son of Añjanā with great devotion.
The wise man, always remembering the means [taught] by the Yogin, once at night remained together with his friend, bestowing all that is desired.
Having gone outside and shaken off that disguise, Kumudākara entered the house of Jīmūtaketu and awakened him.
The gatekeepers approached that brother-in-law Kumudākara, greeted him with respectful welcome, and asked the reason for his arrival. (43)
He said: "Seeing an evil dream regarding his daughter himself, my father, fearing some misfortune, sent me with the message: 'Let your sister be seen. (44)
Thus addressed by him, Jīmūta, filled with anger, said:
"While I am present, who is able to inflict harm upon Padminī?
He replied to that Jīmūta: "O Lord, you should not speak in such a manner."
For a long time, that elephant, seeking a vulnerability, has been intent on carrying off his own sister. || 46 ||
Thus addressed by him, Jīmūta went to the dwelling of his beloved;
there, however, only Milinda remained in the form of Bhramarikā. (47)
"My sister is not to be seen," Kumudākara wept;
Jīmūta, becoming exceedingly enraged, arrived at Mattebhapura.
Kumudākara went there together with his friend;
having hurled his thunderbolt, Jīmūta struck down that intoxicated elephant there.
Then Bhīma, wandering like a cloud, went to the temple of the Kaumudī vow;
but seeing him intoxicated, she fled in fear.
Under the sway of love, that foolish man firmly embraced her who resembled a lotus plant,
and was then cast into a mechanical device situated within it by means of medicinal drugs.
The fire that arose and blazed consumed that evil-minded one;
yet even though burnt by the fire there, Jīmūta did not give up his life.
Having ascended the Kaumudī mansion, she herself saw him wandering in the courtyard of the lotus-pool; she then summoned him privately through her companion.
Having understood that secret, did the powerful son of Mattebhā not take her into his confidence and sport with her day and night? (54)
Seizing the innocent young elephant by force, he began to kill it;
then a mass of snow arrived there and spoke these words to the young elephant: || 55 ||
"For the sake of quickly attaining grace from Bhairavī, this vow is being observed by me;
at its conclusion, a sacrificial offering must be given to her by me, consisting of a young man and a young woman. (56)
"A certain young woman has been pointed out; let this youth be given to her.
Having agreed to that, Kalabha placed him in a prison cell.
Then Milinda, terrified, reached his own city and quickly reported all of that in detail to Kāsāra. || 58 ||
Grieving, he called out to the sun together with his beloved;
as that [sun] approached, a great mass of snow driven by the cold came upon his dear one.
Having realized that Padmanī had indeed vanished, Jahnu concealed his true form; nevertheless, the lake was utterly distressed by the people.
Himānī, sword in hand, first began to slay Padmanī in order to quickly please Bhairavī Kālī with their blood. (61)
Then Lakṣmī approached him for refuge, for she considered him her protector;
Śrī herself, intent on protecting her devotees, quickly went to that Bhāskara. 62.
There, that illustrious one brought [the sword] down upon his neck as it fell;
seizing his beloved by both hands, he quickly drew her away.
Seeing the sun, the great mass of snow fled in haste;
meanwhile, many wonderful serpents were created by the enraged Bhairavī.
While Lakṣmī was looking on, the Lord of Birds appeared from the sky;
with his exceedingly fierce tip of the beak, he of great speed destroyed them.
Then that Bhairavī, her mouth wide open, released a terrifying host of Rākṣasas to bite and tear apart the two sons of Kāsāra.
While Lakṣmī was looking on, the Lord of Monkeys appeared in the sky;
the one of great splendor swiftly struck down those Rākṣasas with his tail.
Bhairavī herself, the beloved of Hari, though possessing a terrifying form, rushed toward them with the intent to slay, yet she was completely filled with compassion. (68)
The Mother, the protectress of her devotees, let out a roar of "huṃ" for the worlds;
terrified by her "huṃ" sound, Bhairavī [approached] her who is affectionate toward her devotees.
Having prostrated, she said, "O Queen of Gods, may my offense be forgiven.
The goddess Bhairavī, the beloved of Hari, being pleased, spoke to her.
"Having placed these [beings] upon this celestial chariot, take them now quickly to the city of Kāsāra by means of the spirits; otherwise, they will not remain unperturbed. (71)
Thus addressed, Bhairavī joyfully accepted her words,
just as the lotus accepts the sun and the night-lily accepts the moon.
Having placed him upon a celestial chariot, Kāsāra,
his mind filled with joy, led him to the temple of Kāsāra along with the yogi Śāradānanda.
Seeing his daughter united with her husband and his son accompanied by his wife, he, filled with curiosity, worshipped Śrī, the mother of the worlds.
Because Rāma belongs to the solar dynasty (Ravivaṃśya), the name Bhāskara is indeed appropriate for him;
and because Lakṣmī, who is a transformation of Sītā, is like a lotus, [the name Padmabhū is] likewise constant [for her]. (75)

Likewise, having placed in his mind the King of Videha—who, due to the identity between those two, was joined with the one called Padminī and whose form was non-different from the lake—[he proceeded]. (76)
In this most enchanting drama, Jīmūta is portrayed as distinct from Rāvaṇa, while Śāradānanda-yogin is likewise distinguished from Kauśika.
In this work, the poet has for the most part indicated the narrative of the Rāmāyaṇa; for instance, he has clearly depicted the episode of Tāṭakā as being pervaded by darkness. (78)
The breaking of Śiva’s bow has been told by way of illustrating the lotus;
in this manner, other stories concerning the Lord of the Raghus should also be inferred by the wise. (72)
Thus ends the Compendium of Tales composed by Varadarāja.

There exists a lake named Kāsāra, which, by virtue of its stainless inner lotuses, removes the distress of those who resort to it; it is the protector of its subjects. Born from that [lake] is Padminī, an abode of modesty, intellect, and beauty.

Even though he has no regard for him, out of gratitude he maintains a sense of courtesy toward him, remembering the assistance rendered by him in the past.

"Oh, how great is the noble one’s cause for anxiety! By some means or other, you are striving to bring those two together.

A rogue elephant is attacking and obstructing [the path] for the sake of his own cub.

honored by them with great affection for their own daughter,

Kāśā: Let her be ushered in with due ceremony. Doorkeeper: [Does so. Kāśā: [Enters. Kāśā: Welcome, noble lady. Please be seated. [She sits. Kāśā: Noble lady, you have been heard of by me for some time. I am pleased to see you in person. What may I do for you? Queen: Mother, I have come to pay my respects to you. Kāśā: Noble lady, you are already honored by your very presence. What further service can I provide? Queen: Mother, I have a request to make. Kāśā: Noble lady, speak. Queen: Mother, I wish to enter the inner apartments. Kāśā: Noble lady, why this haste? Queen: Mother, it is because I am pregnant. Kāśā: Noble lady, what need is there for haste? For women, pregnancy is a source of great joy. Queen: Mother, it is not merely joy; it is a matter of life and death. Kāśā: Noble lady, why such distress? Queen: Mother, it is because I fear the jealousy of my co-wives. Kāśā: Noble lady, who would dare to be jealous of you? Queen: Mother, it is because of the king’s partiality toward them. Kāśā: Noble lady, the king is devoted to you. He will never show favoritism toward others. Queen: Mother, even if he were devoted, he might still act out of partiality. Kāśā: Noble lady, do not speak thus. The king is a man of dharma and will never act contrary to righteousness. Queen: Mother, even if he were a man of dharma, he might still be swayed by passion. Kāśā: Noble lady, do not speak thus. Passion cannot overcome his steadfastness. Queen: Mother, even if his steadfastness were unshakable, I fear the influence of fate. Kāśā: Noble lady, fate is powerless before virtue. Do not fear. Queen: Mother, even if fate were powerless, I fear the gossip of the people. Kāśā: Noble lady, the people will praise you for your virtue. Do not fear. Queen: Mother, even if they praised me, I fear the loss of my reputation. Kāśā: Noble lady, your reputation is secure. It cannot be tarnished. Queen: Mother, even if my reputation were secure, I fear the pain of childbirth. Kāśā: Noble lady, the pain of childbirth is a natural part of a woman's life. It is not something to be feared. Queen: Mother, even if the pain were natural, I fear the separation from my husband. Kāśā: Noble lady, your husband is ever devoted to you. There shall be no separation. Queen: Mother, even if there were no separation, I fear the suffering of being separated from my son. Kāśā: Noble lady, your son will be born healthy and strong. There shall be no suffering. Queen: Mother, even if my son were healthy, I fear the cruelty of my co-wives. Kāśā: Noble lady, your co-wives will be subdued by your virtue. They will not be cruel. Where am I, the foremost of evildoers, and where is this grace of yours that is obtained here through meritorious deeds?

"O son of the Wind, do not be angry thinking, 'He is indeed binding me';

Intellect, strength, fame, fortitude, fearlessness, and health;

Child Kāśastamba! The intoxicated Jīmūta has ceased his assault, having slain that wicked elephant.

Kāśyapa, too, being free from all taint, was filled with joy upon seeing his beloved son Bhāskara; his lotus-like face blossomed with delight at beholding his own daughter, who had attained the stainless moonlight,
and he rejoiced as the father of Bhāskara at the rising of his own son.
Udayadhara and Kāmāra:
"O Blessed One! All is well through your power.
Śāra—
By the grace of the Blessed Indirā—
she by whose favor the Moon-crested Lord, having obtained his bow Pināka, shines resplendent—
who is she that dwells in the lotus, whose praise is clearly proclaimed by the Vedic hymn, and by which immortal would she not be worshipped?
By the Yajus mantra "asye...na," she is praised all the more;
what other goddess is heard of who could be the Mother of the World without her?
By the mantra "Gandhadvārā," she who is called the Sovereign of all beings (Sarvabhūteśvarī) is praised; apart from Lakṣmī, what other protector of beings exists?
When her own lord, named Rāma, had appeared within the lineage of the Sun,
she was born on earth in the house of Janaka; while wandering there with her friends,
after some time had passed, she took refuge in that very lord.
I take refuge in her who became the cause for the destruction of the multitude of wicked arrows.
Just as a mother, enduring even the pain in her breasts, suckles her own child with milk,
so too did Sītā, enduring the agony caused by the night-stalker, bring joy to the world through the intoxication of the Ten-faced One’s destruction.
What more need be said?

Whether one be a god or a human, how could one be truly fortunate without remembering and bowing to that blessed Goddess who is solely intent on protecting her devotees through her compassion? We are indeed blessed to do so.
Kāśyapa: You have spoken the truth.
Uda—
May there be eternal auspiciousness from Janaki and Raghunatha, who themselves are the parents of the worlds, ever vigilant in protecting the universe.
Bhāskara:

May there be auspiciousness for the son of the Wind, who is uniquely skilled in punishing wicked Rākṣasas, the destroyer of the [ten] senses, and the one who bears the burden of protecting the virtuous.
May there always be auspiciousness for the great sovereign of all birds, whose pride the serpents have destroyed by the flapping of his wings.
Aruṇa:— (Embraces Bhāskara) Milinda:—
(He embraces Kumudākara.
(Everyone looks at one another with curiosity.
Śāra—
"Bhāskara! What further favor may I bestow upon you?
Bhāskara:

"O Lord, through your unimpeded grace, I have attained steadfastness on the path of the virtuous; I am ever filled with all perfections in this purifying state, and all my calamities have been destroyed."

O Lord, served by the masters of yoga, O Master who has conquered the senses through fortitude, the marriage of Padminī has taken place without obstacle; O Blessed One, everything auspicious has been attained by me.
Nevertheless, let this be: (Bharata-vākya) May the gods on earth flourish, ever devoted to the true dharma and radiant with fame;
may kings be intent upon honoring the gods of the earth; and may the virtuous live for a long time.
May the supreme subjects and cattle here rejoice; may the earth be radiant with crops;
and may devotion to King Sundara flourish in the heart of Rāma.
Thus ends the tenth act in the *Padminīpariṇaya*.
Homage to the messenger of Rāma.
May it be auspicious!
